# 3.4 First Hop Redundancy (HSRP and VRRP)

> **Blueprint 3.4:** Interpret the operational status of First Hop Redundancy Protocols (HSRP and VRRP)

## Summary

A host has one default gateway. If that router fails, the host is cut off. A first hop redundancy protocol (FHRP) lets two routers share one virtual IP and virtual MAC. One forwards, the other takes over within seconds, and the hosts change nothing. Think of a duty phone number: it rings whoever is on shift.

## Key facts and defaults

| Item | HSRP | VRRP |
|---|---|---|
| Standard | Cisco proprietary | Open standard |
| Roles | Active, Standby | Master, Backup |
| Default priority | 100 | 100 |
| Winner | Highest priority, then highest IP | Same |
| Pre-emption | Off | On |
| Timers | Hello 3 s, hold 10 s | Advertisement 1 s |
| Multicast | 224.0.0.2 (v1), 224.0.0.102 (v2) | 224.0.0.18 |
| Carried in | UDP 1985 | IP protocol 112 |
| Virtual MAC | 0000.0c07.acXX (v1), 0000.0c9f.fXXX (v2) | 0000.5e00.01XX |
| Virtual IP | Spare address in the subnet | Can be a router's real IP |

- XX is the group number in **hex**: group 10 is `0a`.
- HSRP states: Initial, Learn, Listen, Speak, Standby, Active.
- The VRRP address owner (its real IP is the virtual IP) has priority 255.

## IOS commands

Configuration is not asked for. Recognise these lines, because they explain the output.

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `show standby brief` | One line per HSRP group |
| `show standby` | Full HSRP detail |
| `show vrrp brief` | One line per VRRP group |
| `standby 10 ip 192.168.10.1` | Group 10 virtual IP |
| `standby 10 priority 110` | Raises priority |
| `standby 10 preempt` | Can take Active back |

## Verification

Columns in the two brief outputs are narrowed to fit.

```
SW1# show standby brief
                    P indicates configured to preempt.
                    |
Interface  Grp  Pri P State   Active        Standby       Virtual IP
Vl10       10   110 P Active  local         192.168.10.3  192.168.10.1
Vl20       20   100   Standby 192.168.20.3  local         192.168.20.1
```

```
SW1# show standby vlan 10
Vlan10 - Group 10
  State is Active
    2 state changes, last state change 00:12:45
  Virtual IP address is 192.168.10.1
  Active virtual MAC address is 0000.0c07.ac0a
    Local virtual MAC address is 0000.0c07.ac0a (v1 default)
  Hello time 3 sec, hold time 10 sec
    Next hello sent in 1.264 secs
  Preemption enabled
  Active router is local
  Standby router is 192.168.10.3, priority 100 (expires in 9.872 sec)
  Priority 110 (configured 110)
  Group name is "hsrp-Vl10-10" (default)
```

```
R2# show vrrp brief
Interface   Grp Pri Time  Own Pre State   Master addr   Group addr
Gi0/1       1   100 3609       Y  Backup  192.168.30.2  192.168.30.1
```

What to look for:

- **State:** one Active (or Master) per group. `local` means this device. SW1 forwards for VLAN 10 and backs up VLAN 20.
- **Pri and P:** with 110 and pre-emption, SW1 takes group 10 back after a reboot.
- **Virtual IP:** the same on both routers, and the hosts' default gateway.
- **VRRP:** R2 is Backup, the Master is 192.168.30.2 and `Group addr` is the virtual IP. `Pre` Y: pre-emption on. `Own` blank: R2 is not the owner.

## Exam traps

- A higher-priority router in Standby is normal in HSRP without `preempt`, if it joined late.
- Both routers Active with Standby `unknown`: they cannot hear each other. Suspect layer 2, the VLAN or mixed HSRP versions.
- `Priority 100 (configured 110)`: lowered, usually by a tracked interface going down.
- HSRP v1 and v2 do not work together.
- VRRP output layout varies by IOS version. Find the state, priority and master address.

## On real sites

A Meraki MX warm spare pair and a Peplink high availability pair both use VRRP: two units, one shared gateway address, heartbeats across the LAN. The site fault is the same everywhere: if the patching or VLAN between the units is wrong, no heartbeats arrive and both claim the gateway.

## Self-test

1. In the brief output above, which device forwards for VLAN 20?
2. What is the HSRP version 1 virtual MAC for group 20?
3. R1 (priority 150) reboots while R2 (100) is Active. No `preempt`. Who is Active after, and in VRRP?
4. Both routers show Active with Standby `unknown`. What does that mean?
5. Give three differences between HSRP and VRRP.

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The other router, 192.168.20.3. SW1 is Standby.
2. 0000.0c07.ac14, because 20 is 14 in hex.
3. R2 stays Active. VRRP pre-empts by default, so R1 would become Master.
4. They cannot hear each other's hellos. Check the VLAN and cabling between them.
5. Any three: proprietary or open, role names, pre-emption off or on, timers, multicast address, virtual MAC.

</details>

title: 4.1 Local Users and AAA (TACACS+ and RADIUS)

# 4.1 Local Users and AAA (TACACS+ and RADIUS)

> **Blueprint 4.1:** Configure network devices with local usernames and as an AAA client (TACACS+ and RADIUS) for management

## Summary

Every engineer should log in to a router or switch with their own username, over SSH. Small sites keep the usernames on the device (the local database). Larger networks make each device an AAA client of a central TACACS+ or RADIUS server, so one account works everywhere and is disabled in one place. A local user stays as the fallback. Think of a gatehouse: the guard phones head office to check your pass, and uses the paper list in the drawer only when the line is dead.

## Key facts and defaults

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| AAA | Authentication, authorisation, accounting |
| TACACS+ | TCP 49. Encrypts the whole payload. Separates the three A's. Device administration |
| RADIUS | UDP 1812 and 1813 (legacy 1645, 1646). Encrypts only the password. Network access |
| Privilege levels | 0 to 15. 1 is user EXEC, 15 is full access |
| `secret` | Stored as a hash. `password` is clear text |
| Method list | Methods tried in order. The next is used only if the one before does not answer |

## IOS commands

Local users and SSH:

```
hostname R1
ip domain name example.com
crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048
username admin privilege 15 secret Str0ngPass
ip ssh version 2
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input ssh
```

AAA client. Create the local user first:

```
aaa new-model
tacacs server TAC1
 address ipv4 10.1.1.50
 key SharedKey1
radius server RAD1
 address ipv4 10.1.1.51 auth-port 1812 acct-port 1813
 key SharedKey2
! default list: used by every line unless told otherwise
aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ local
aaa authorization exec default group tacacs+ local
! named list: only used where it is applied
aaa authentication login CONSOLE local
line con 0
 login authentication CONSOLE
```

For RADIUS, write `group radius` in place of `group tacacs+`. The key must match the server's.

## Verification

```
R1#show ip ssh
SSH Enabled - version 2.0
Authentication methods:publickey,keyboard-interactive,password
Authentication timeout: 120 secs; Authentication retries: 3
```

(Other lines omitted. They vary by release.)

What to look for:

- `SSH Enabled`. If disabled, the RSA keys are missing.
- `version 2.0`. Version 1.99 means insecure SSH v1 is still accepted.
- Then prove the fallback: log in with the server reachable, and again with it unreachable.

## Exam traps

- `local` is used only when no server answers. If the server answers "reject", the login fails and `local` is not tried.
- `aaa new-model` changes how every line authenticates at once. Without a local user you can lock yourself out.
- The `default` list applies to all lines automatically. A named list does nothing until `login authentication NAME` is on the line.
- `crypto key generate rsa` fails until a hostname and domain name are set.
- `login` checks the line password. `login local` checks the username database.

## On real sites

Your personal login to the Meraki dashboard or InControl is the cloud version of this: named users held centrally, not on each box. You have met RADIUS when setting a Meraki SSID to WPA2-Enterprise, where you enter the server address, port 1812 and a shared secret. IOS needs the same three items under `radius server`.

## Self-test

1. A router has `aaa authentication login default group tacacs+ local`. The server replies that the password is wrong. Is the local database tried?
2. Give three differences between TACACS+ and RADIUS.
3. List the steps to enable SSH version 2 on a new router.
4. You create a method list called ADMINS, but vty logins still use the default list. What is missing?
5. Why create a local username before typing `aaa new-model`?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. No. A reject is an answer, so the login fails. `local` is used only when no server responds.
2. TACACS+: TCP 49, encrypts the whole payload, separates the three A's. RADIUS: UDP 1812 and 1813, encrypts only the password, combines authentication and authorisation.
3. Hostname, domain name, RSA keys (modulus 2048), a username with a secret, `ip ssh version 2`, then `login local` and `transport input ssh` on the vty lines.
4. `login authentication ADMINS` under `line vty 0 4`.
5. AAA takes over every line at once. If the server cannot be reached, the local user is the only way in.

</details>

title: 4.2 Secure File Transfer (SCP and SFTP)
md:
# 4.2 Secure File Transfer (SCP and SFTP)

> **Blueprint 4.2:** Manage device configuration and software files using secure file transfer operations with SFTP/SCP

## Summary

A router or switch holds two kinds of file you must look after: configurations (back up, restore) and software images (copy in before an upgrade). TFTP has no login and FTP sends the password in clear text. SCP and SFTP run inside SSH, so the login and the file are encrypted. It is the difference between posting a spare key in a clear bag and in a locked courier box.

## Key facts and defaults

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| SCP and SFTP | TCP 22. Both run over SSH |
| SCP | Simple copy of a file in or out |
| SFTP | Fuller file protocol. Not related to FTP |
| TFTP | UDP 69. No login, no encryption |
| FTP | TCP 20 and 21. Login, but clear text |
| IOS SCP server | Off until `ip scp server enable` |
| Copy to running-config | Merges with what is there |
| Copy to startup-config | Replaces the file |

## IOS commands

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `copy running-config scp:` | Backs up the config to a server |
| `copy scp: flash:` | Pulls a file, such as an image |
| `copy sftp: flash:` | The same pull using SFTP |
| `ip scp server enable` | Device accepts SCP copies from a PC |
| `dir flash:` | Lists files and free space |
| `verify /md5 flash:FILE` | Calculates a file's MD5 hash |

The device as client. IOS prompts for anything you leave out:

```
R1#copy running-config scp:
Address or name of remote host []? 10.1.1.50
Destination username [R1]? backup
Destination filename [r1-confg]? r1-backup.cfg
Writing r1-backup.cfg
Password:
!
3184 bytes copied in 3.980 secs (800 bytes/sec)
```

One line, this time pulling an image:

```
R1#copy scp://backup@10.1.1.50/iosxe-17.9.4.bin flash:
```

The device as SCP server. SSH must already work (see 4.1):

```
aaa new-model
aaa authentication login default local
aaa authorization exec default local
username admin privilege 15 secret Str0ngPass
ip scp server enable
```

Many IOS XE routers call the main file system `bootflash:`. Check with `dir`.

## Verification

```
R1#dir flash:
Directory of flash:/

   12  -rw-   706422748  Jan 15 2027 10:42:17 +00:00  iosxe-17.9.4.bin
   13  -rw-        3184  Jan 15 2027 10:51:03 +00:00  r1-backup.cfg

7693897728 bytes total (5312245760 bytes free)

R1#verify /md5 flash:iosxe-17.9.4.bin
..............................Done!
verify /md5 (flash:iosxe-17.9.4.bin) = 7f2c9a51e0b84d36a1c5f09e2d7b6c48
```

What to look for:

- Before the copy: `bytes free` is larger than the file.
- After the copy: the size matches the size on the server.
- The MD5 hash matches the one on Cisco's download page. If not, the copy is corrupt. Copy it again.

## Exam traps

- SFTP is not FTP and not FTPS. It is a separate protocol inside SSH on TCP 22.
- `ip scp server enable` is needed only when the device is the server. `copy scp:` from the device works without it.
- Copying to `running-config` merges. Old lines the file does not mention stay in place.
- SCP to the device fails if SSH is not working or the user does not reach privilege 15.

## On real sites

Meraki and Peplink hide this job: the dashboard and InControl push firmware and keep the configuration in the cloud. On IOS you do it by hand. Back up the config before any change and copy the new image into flash yourself. A laptop running an SSH server is enough for a cabinet visit.

## Self-test

1. Which port do SCP and SFTP use, and why?
2. Which command starts a backup of the running config to an SCP server?
3. You copy a saved config from a server to `running-config`. Is the running config replaced?
4. SSH logins to a router work, but a PC cannot push a file to it with SCP. Name two things to check.
5. Name two checks to make after copying a new image into flash.

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. TCP 22. Both run inside an SSH session, so they share its port, login and encryption.
2. `copy running-config scp:` then answer the prompts for host, username and file name.
3. No, it is merged. Lines not in the file stay.
4. `ip scp server enable` is configured, and the user reaches privilege 15.
5. `dir flash:` to confirm the size, and `verify /md5` to compare the hash with the published value.

</details>

title: 4.3 NAT and PAT
md:
# 4.3 NAT and PAT

> **Blueprint 4.3:** Configure NAT/PAT on IOS XE routers

## Summary

Private (RFC 1918) addresses cannot be routed on the internet, so the edge router rewrites them to public addresses on the way out and back again on the way in. That is NAT. PAT is the common form: every inside host shares one public address and the router tells the sessions apart by port number. Think of an office with one public phone number. The switchboard knows which extension made each call, so the reply reaches the right desk.

## Key facts and defaults

| Term | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Inside local | Private address of the inside host | 10.1.1.21 |
| Inside global | Public address it is translated to | 203.0.113.1 |
| Outside global | Real address of the internet host | 198.51.100.7 |
| Outside local | How that host appears from inside (usually the same) | 198.51.100.7 |

Inside or outside says where the host is. Local or global says where the address is seen from.

| Type | Mapping | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Static NAT | One to one, permanent | Server reached from outside |
| Dynamic NAT | One to one, from a pool | Rare today |
| PAT (overload) | Many to one, by port | Normal internet access |

## IOS commands

```
! 1. Mark the interfaces (needed for every type)
interface g0/0/0
 ip nat inside
interface g0/0/1
 ip nat outside

! 2. Static NAT
ip nat inside source static 10.1.1.10 203.0.113.10

! 3. Dynamic NAT: the ACL picks who is translated
access-list 1 permit 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255
ip nat pool PUBLIC 203.0.113.20 203.0.113.30 netmask 255.255.255.0
ip nat inside source list 1 pool PUBLIC

! 4. PAT, used in place of step 3: share the WAN address
ip nat inside source list 1 interface g0/0/1 overload
```

To overload a pool, add `overload` to the end of the step 3 command.

## Verification

```
R1#show ip nat translations
Pro Inside global     Inside local    Outside local    Outside global
--- 203.0.113.10      10.1.1.10       ---              ---
tcp 203.0.113.1:51000 10.1.1.21:51000 198.51.100.7:443 198.51.100.7:443
tcp 203.0.113.1:52144 10.1.1.22:52144 198.51.100.7:443 198.51.100.7:443

R1#show ip nat statistics
Total active translations: 3 (1 static, 2 dynamic; 2 extended)
Outside interfaces:
  GigabitEthernet0/0/1
Inside interfaces:
  GigabitEthernet0/0/0
Hits: 418  Misses: 2
```

(Columns closed up to fit a phone screen.)

What to look for:

- The static entry is always there and has no ports. PAT entries show ports and appear only while traffic flows.
- Two inside hosts share one inside global address: overload is working.
- The right interfaces are listed as inside and outside.

## Exam traps

- No translations at all: `ip nat inside` or `ip nat outside` is missing or swapped. IOS gives no warning.
- ACL does not match (wrong network or wildcard), so hosts are never translated. In a NAT ACL, `permit` means "translate this".
- `overload` forgotten: each host takes a whole pool address. When the pool is used up, the next host fails.
- Static NAT lets the outside start a connection. Dynamic NAT and PAT entries are created only by inside traffic.
- IOS refuses to remove a pool or rule that is in use. Run `clear ip nat translation *` first.

## On real sites

A Meraki MX or a Peplink router does PAT on its WAN port out of the box, which is why you have rarely had to think about it. Their port forwarding and 1:1 NAT rules are static NAT under another name. On IOS nothing is automatic: you mark the interfaces, write the ACL and add the rule yourself.

## Self-test

1. Host 10.1.1.21 is translated to 203.0.113.1 to reach server 198.51.100.7. Name the inside local, inside global and outside global addresses.
2. A pool holds 203.0.113.20 to 203.0.113.30 with no `overload`. How many inside hosts can be online at once?
3. The configuration looks right but `show ip nat translations` stays empty. Give three things to check.
4. Write the static NAT command that publishes server 10.1.1.10 as 203.0.113.10.
5. IOS will not delete a NAT pool because it is in use. What do you do?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Inside local 10.1.1.21, inside global 203.0.113.1, outside global 198.51.100.7.
2. Eleven. Each host needs its own pool address, so the twelfth fails.
3. `ip nat inside` and `ip nat outside` are on the right interfaces, the ACL matches the inside local addresses, and traffic is really reaching the router.
4. `ip nat inside source static 10.1.1.10 203.0.113.10`
5. Run `clear ip nat translation *`, then remove the pool.

</details>

title: 4.4 DNS Records and Name Resolution Faults
md:
# 4.4 DNS Records and Name Resolution Faults

> **Blueprint 4.4:** Diagnose issues with DNS records (A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, NS, and PTR) to support host, web application, and mail server access by name

## Summary

DNS is the phone book of the network: people use names, packets need addresses. Each record type answers a different question. When a record is missing, wrong or out of date, the network is healthy but users say "the server is down". Prove it is DNS, not routing, then find the record at fault.

## Key facts and defaults

| Record | Answers |
|---|---|
| A | Name to IPv4 address |
| AAAA | Name to IPv6 address |
| CNAME | Alias to another name, never to an IP |
| MX | Mail server for a domain. Lowest preference first |
| NS | Authoritative name server for a zone |
| PTR | IP address back to a name |

By symptom:

| Symptom | Suspect | Check |
|---|---|---|
| IP works, no name resolves | Client DNS setting or port 53 blocked | `ipconfig /all` |
| One name "Non-existent domain" | A record missing or mistyped | `nslookup NAME` |
| Name gives the old IP | Stale A record or cached answer | `ipconfig /flushdns` |
| Dual-stack PCs fail or lag | Wrong AAAA record | `nslookup -type=aaaa` |
| Alias fails, real name works | CNAME target wrong | `nslookup ALIAS` |
| Web fine, inbound mail fails | MX missing or target wrong | `nslookup -type=mx` |
| Domain dead from outside | NS or delegation wrong | `nslookup -type=ns` |
| Our mail rejected by others | PTR missing or wrong | `nslookup IP` |

## IOS commands

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `ip name-server 10.1.1.5` | DNS server the device itself asks |
| `show hosts` | Name servers and known names |
| `ping www.example.com` | Quick test that a name resolves |

## Verification

```
C:\>nslookup www.example.com
Server:  dns1.example.com
Address:  10.1.1.5

Name:    web01.example.com
Address:  203.0.113.80
Aliases:  www.example.com

C:\>nslookup -type=mx example.com
Server:  dns1.example.com
Address:  10.1.1.5

example.com     MX preference = 10, mail exchanger = mail1.example.com
example.com     MX preference = 20, mail exchanger = mail2.example.com

C:\>nslookup hr.example.com
Server:  dns1.example.com
Address:  10.1.1.5

*** dns1.example.com can't find hr.example.com: Non-existent domain
```

What to look for:

- `Server` is the DNS server that answered. A wrong one is a client setting fault.
- `Aliases`: www is a CNAME. `Name` is the real host and needs its own A record.
- "Non-existent domain": the server answered but has no such record.

## Exam traps

- MX: lowest number wins. It must point to a host name with an A or AAAA record, not to an IP address or a CNAME.
- PTR records live in a separate reverse zone. Adding an A record does not create the PTR.
- After a fix, clients keep the old answer until its TTL runs out. That is caching, not a second fault.

## On real sites

A Meraki AP or switch that has an IP address but cannot resolve names cannot reach the dashboard, so a bad DNS server handed out by DHCP can take a site "offline" while the cabling is fine. Your first test on site is the exam's too: ping a public IP address, then ping a name. If only the name fails, stop checking cables.

## Self-test

1. Users reach a server by IP but not by name. Routing or DNS, and what do you check first?
2. example.com has MX 10 mail1 and MX 20 mail2. Which is tried first, and what must mail1 have?
3. A website loads on IPv4-only PCs, but dual-stack laptops wait a long time first. Which record?
4. A partner rejects mail from 203.0.113.25 because the reverse lookup fails. Which record is missing?
5. You corrected an A record, but some PCs still reach the old address. Why?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. DNS. Check which DNS server the client uses (`ipconfig /all`), then query the name with `nslookup`.
2. mail1, because the lowest preference is tried first. It must have its own A or AAAA record.
3. AAAA. Dual-stack clients try IPv6 first, so a wrong AAAA sends them to a dead address.
4. The PTR record for 203.0.113.25, in the reverse zone.
5. They cached the old answer and its TTL has not expired. Run `ipconfig /flushdns` or wait.

</details>

title: 4.5 IPsec VPNs (Remote Access and Site-to-Site)
md:
# 4.5 IPsec VPNs (Remote Access and Site-to-Site)

> **Blueprint 4.5:** Describe IPsec remote access and site-to-site VPNs (protocols and transport modes)

## Summary

A VPN carries private traffic across a network you do not trust, usually the internet. IPsec is the standard set of protocols that does this at Layer 3. It gives four services: confidentiality (encryption), integrity (hashing), origin authentication (pre-shared keys or certificates) and anti-replay. Think of an armoured van between two depots: the road is public, but nobody can read, alter or re-send the load.

## Key facts and defaults

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| IKE | UDP 500. Authenticates the peers, agrees keys |
| NAT traversal | UDP 4500. ESP wrapped in UDP |
| ESP | IP protocol 50. Encryption, integrity, authentication |
| AH | IP protocol 51. Integrity and authentication, no encryption |
| Tunnel mode | Whole original packet protected, new IP header added. Site-to-site |
| Transport mode | Original IP header kept, only payload protected. Host to host, GRE over IPsec |

| | Site-to-site | Remote access |
|---|---|---|
| Ends | Router or firewall at each site | User device and a VPN gateway |
| Software | None on the hosts | VPN client on the device |
| When up | Permanent | On demand |

A tunnel comes up in two stages. IKE authenticates the peers and builds a secure channel. Through it they agree the security associations (SAs): the keys and algorithms that protect the data.

## IOS commands

No configuration is in scope for this objective. Recognise these show commands:

| Command | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| `show crypto isakmp sa` | IKEv1 peer state. `QM_IDLE` is healthy |
| `show crypto ikev2 sa` | The same for IKEv2 |
| `show crypto ipsec sa` | Data SAs and packet counters |

## Verification

For recognition only:

```
R1#show crypto isakmp sa
IPv4 Crypto ISAKMP SA
dst             src             state          conn-id status
198.51.100.2    203.0.113.1     QM_IDLE           1001 ACTIVE

R1#show crypto ipsec sa
   local  ident (addr/mask/prot/port): (10.1.1.0/255.255.255.0/0/0)
   remote ident (addr/mask/prot/port): (10.2.2.0/255.255.255.0/0/0)
    #pkts encaps: 152, #pkts encrypt: 152, #pkts digest: 152
    #pkts decaps: 148, #pkts decrypt: 148, #pkts verify: 148
```

(Extract. The full output is much longer.)

What to look for:

- `QM_IDLE` and `ACTIVE`: the IKE stage is complete.
- The `ident` lines: the private subnets being protected.
- `encaps` and `decaps` both rising: traffic flows both ways. Decaps stuck at zero means nothing is coming back.

## Exam traps

- AH does not encrypt. If the question says confidentiality, the answer is ESP.
- ESP and AH are IP protocol numbers (50 and 51), not ports. IKE is UDP 500.
- AH fails across NAT, because NAT changes the IP header that AH protects. ESP crosses NAT using NAT traversal on UDP 4500.
- Tunnel mode adds a new IP header. Transport mode keeps the original.
- GRE on its own encrypts nothing.

## On real sites

Meraki Auto VPN is site-to-site IPsec with the hard part hidden: the dashboard works out the peers and keys. When you add a non-Meraki peer you see the real settings, such as IKE version, pre-shared key and private subnets. Peplink SpeedFusion is Peplink's own site-to-site VPN and plays the same role.

## Self-test

1. Which IPsec protocol provides encryption, and what is its IP protocol number?
2. What happens to the original IP header in tunnel mode and in transport mode?
3. Why does AH fail across NAT, and how does ESP get across?
4. A home worker's laptop and a branch office both connect to head office. Which VPN type suits each?
5. A firewall sits between two IPsec gateways. What must it permit?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. ESP, IP protocol 50. AH (51) gives integrity and authentication only.
2. Tunnel mode protects it and adds a new IP header. Transport mode keeps it and protects only the payload.
3. NAT changes the IP header that AH protects, so the check fails. ESP is wrapped in UDP 4500 (NAT traversal).
4. Remote access for the laptop (client software). Site-to-site for the branch (gateway to gateway).
5. UDP 500 for IKE, IP protocol 50 for ESP, and UDP 4500 if NAT is in the path.

</details>

title: 4.6 IPv4 Access Control Lists
md:
# 4.6 IPv4 Access Control Lists

> **Blueprint 4.6:** Configure IPv4 access control lists (standard, extended, numbered, and named ACLs)

## Summary

An ACL is an ordered list of permit and deny lines that a router checks packets against. It works like a doorman with a list: he reads from the top, acts on the first line that fits, and turns away anyone not listed. A standard ACL looks only at the source address. An extended ACL also looks at protocol, destination and port. An ACL does nothing until it is applied to an interface or to the vty lines.

## Key facts and defaults

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Standard numbers | 1 to 99 and 1300 to 1999 |
| Extended numbers | 100 to 199 and 2000 to 2699 |
| Order | Top down, first match wins |
| Last line | Implicit `deny any`, never shown |
| Limit | One ACL per interface, per direction, per protocol |
| Placement | Standard near the destination. Extended near the source |
| Sequence numbers | Start at 10, step 10 |

**Wildcard masks.** A 0 bit means "must match", a 1 bit means "ignore". Take each octet of the subnet mask from 255.

| Prefix | Subnet mask | Wildcard |
|---|---|---|
| /24 | 255.255.255.0 | 0.0.0.255 |
| /26 | 255.255.255.192 | 0.0.0.63 |
| /28 | 255.255.255.240 | 0.0.0.15 |
| /30 | 255.255.255.252 | 0.0.0.3 |
| /20 | 255.255.240.0 | 0.0.15.255 |

- 192.168.10.64/26: 255 minus 192 is 63, so `192.168.10.64 0.0.0.63` matches 192.168.10.64 to 192.168.10.127.
- 172.16.32.0/20: 255 minus 240 is 15, so `172.16.32.0 0.0.15.255` matches 172.16.32.0 to 172.16.47.255.
- `host 10.2.2.5` means wildcard 0.0.0.0. `any` means every address.

## IOS commands

```
! Standard numbered (source only)
access-list 10 permit 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255

! Extended numbered
access-list 110 permit tcp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.2.2.5 eq 443
access-list 110 deny ip 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 10.2.2.0 0.0.0.255
access-list 110 permit ip any any

! Named extended: the same three rules
ip access-list extended WEB-ONLY
 permit tcp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.2.2.5 eq 443
 deny ip 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 10.2.2.0 0.0.0.255
 permit ip any any

! Edit by sequence number: insert line 15, replace line 30
ip access-list extended WEB-ONLY
 15 permit udp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.2.2.5 eq 53
 no 30
 30 permit ip any any log

! Apply to an interface
interface g0/0/0
 ip access-group WEB-ONLY in

! Apply to the vty lines: who may SSH to this device
line vty 0 4
 access-class 10 in
```

## Verification

```
R1#show access-lists
Standard IP access list 10
    10 permit 10.1.1.0, wildcard bits 0.0.0.255 (12 matches)
Extended IP access list WEB-ONLY
    10 permit tcp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.2.2.5 eq 443 (57 matches)
    15 permit udp 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 host 10.2.2.5 eq domain
    20 deny ip 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255 10.2.2.0 0.0.0.255 (4 matches)
    30 permit ip any any log (1320 matches)

R1#show ip interface g0/0/0 | include access list
  Outgoing Common access list is not set
  Outgoing access list is not set
  Inbound Common access list is not set
  Inbound  access list is WEB-ONLY
```

What to look for:

- The order of the lines. A broad line above a specific one hides it.
- Match counters. A line with no matches (15 here) is not being hit.
- The ACL is applied to the right interface, in the right direction.

## Exam traps

- Every ACL ends with a hidden `deny any`. An ACL with only deny lines blocks everything.
- A `deny ip any any` or `permit ip any any` placed early makes every later line useless.
- Wildcard, not subnet mask. `10.1.1.0 255.255.255.0` in an ACL is wrong.
- To match a port you must name `tcp` or `udp`, not `ip`. For traffic to a server, `eq` goes after the destination.
- `ip access-group` goes on interfaces, `access-class` on vty lines. `in` means traffic arriving on that interface.

## On real sites

Meraki and Peplink firewall rules are also read top down with the first match winning, so the logic is familiar. The big difference is the ending: their outbound rule lists finish with a default allow, while an IOS ACL finishes with a hidden deny. An IOS ACL is also stateless, so replies must be permitted too. The Meraki MX firewall lets return traffic back automatically.

## Self-test

1. Give the wildcard mask for 172.16.32.0/20 and the range it matches.
2. Write a standard ACL that lets only 10.1.1.0/24 SSH to the router, and apply it.
3. Where should a standard ACL be placed, and why?
4. An ACL reads `10 deny ip any any` then `20 permit tcp any any eq 443`. What happens to HTTPS traffic?
5. How do you add a rule between lines 10 and 20 of a named ACL?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. 0.0.15.255. It matches 172.16.32.0 to 172.16.47.255.
2. `access-list 10 permit 10.1.1.0 0.0.0.255`, then `line vty 0 4` and `access-class 10 in`.
3. Close to the destination. It filters on source only, so near the source it would cut that host off from everything.
4. It is dropped. Line 10 matches first and line 20 is never reached.
5. Enter `ip access-list extended NAME` and type the rule with a sequence number in between, such as `15 permit ...`.

</details>

title: 4.7 Layer 2 Security Features
md:
# 4.7 Layer 2 Security Features

> **Blueprint 4.7:** Configure Layer 2 security features: 4.7.a DHCP snooping, 4.7.b Dynamic ARP inspection, 4.7.c Storm control, 4.7.d RA guard, 4.7.e Port security

## Summary

By default a switch port trusts whatever is plugged into it. Anyone at a desk outlet can run a rogue DHCP server, answer ARP for the gateway, flood the VLAN or pretend to be the IPv6 router. These five features take that trust away from host-facing ports and keep it only on uplinks and server ports. Think of a building where every door needs a badge except the loading bay used by known suppliers (the uplink).

## Key facts and defaults

| Feature | Stops | Default |
|---|---|---|
| DHCP snooping | Rogue DHCP servers | Off. All ports untrusted |
| Dynamic ARP Inspection | ARP spoofing | Off. All ports untrusted |
| Storm control | Broadcast, multicast, unknown-unicast floods | Off. Action: drop the excess |
| RA guard | Rogue IPv6 Router Advertisements | Off |
| Port security | Unknown or too many MACs | Off. Maximum 1, shutdown, sticky off |

Port security violation modes:

| Mode | Extra MACs | Port |
|---|---|---|
| protect | Dropped silently | Stays up |
| restrict | Dropped, logged, counted | Stays up |
| shutdown | Dropped, logged, counted | err-disabled |

## IOS commands

**DHCP snooping.** Server messages (OFFER, ACK) arriving on untrusted ports are dropped. The switch builds a binding table (MAC, IP, VLAN, port) from the leases it sees.

```
ip dhcp snooping
ip dhcp snooping vlan 10
interface g1/0/24
 ip dhcp snooping trust
interface range g1/0/1 - 20
 ip dhcp snooping limit rate 15
```

**Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI).** ARP packets on untrusted ports are checked against the snooping binding table. Invalid IP-to-MAC claims are dropped.

```
ip arp inspection vlan 10
interface g1/0/24
 ip arp inspection trust
```

**Storm control.** Limits flooded traffic on a port, here to a percentage of its bandwidth.

```
interface g1/0/5
 storm-control broadcast level 10
 storm-control multicast level 10
 storm-control action shutdown
```

**RA guard.** Drops Router Advertisements arriving on host-facing ports, so only the real router can announce itself as the IPv6 gateway. Apply it to access ports, not to the port facing the router.

```
ipv6 nd raguard policy HOSTS
 device-role host
interface g1/0/5
 ipv6 nd raguard attach-policy HOSTS
```

**Port security.** Limits which and how many MAC addresses may use a port.

```
interface g1/0/5
 switchport mode access
 switchport port-security
 switchport port-security maximum 2
 switchport port-security mac-address sticky
 switchport port-security violation restrict
```

## Verification

```
SW1#show ip dhcp snooping
Switch DHCP snooping is enabled
DHCP snooping is configured on following VLANs:
10
DHCP snooping is operational on following VLANs:
10
Insertion of option 82 is enabled

Interface                  Trusted    Allow option    Rate limit (pps)
-----------------------    -------    ------------    ----------------
GigabitEthernet1/0/24      yes        yes             unlimited

SW1#show port-security interface g1/0/5
Port Security              : Enabled
Port Status                : Secure-up
Violation Mode             : Restrict
Maximum MAC Addresses      : 2
Total MAC Addresses        : 2
Sticky MAC Addresses       : 2
Last Source Address:Vlan   : 0050.56ab.1c2d:10
Security Violation Count   : 3
```

(Some lines omitted from both outputs.)

What to look for:

- Snooping is enabled and operational on the VLAN, and the uplink is trusted.
- `Port Status`: `Secure-up` is normal, `Secure-shutdown` means err-disabled.
- A rising `Security Violation Count`: an extra device is on that port.
- Also know `show ip dhcp snooping binding`, `show ip arp inspection vlan 10`, `show storm-control` and `show interfaces status err-disabled`.

## Exam traps

- DHCP snooping needs the global command and the VLAN command. If the port towards the DHCP server is not trusted, no client gets an address.
- DAI depends on the snooping binding table. A host with a static IP has no binding, so its ARP is dropped unless you add an ARP ACL or trust the port.
- Port security does nothing until the plain `switchport port-security` command is entered. It is rejected on a dynamic port, so set `switchport mode access` first.
- Only shutdown mode err-disables the port. Remove the extra device, then `shutdown` and `no shutdown`.
- Sticky MACs are written to the running config. Save it or they are lost at reload.
- Storm control drops the excess by default. It shuts the port only with `storm-control action shutdown`.

## On real sites

You have seen the faults these features prevent. Someone plugs a home router into a desk outlet and half the floor picks up 192.168.1.x addresses: DHCP snooping stops that. A small unmanaged switch appears under a desk: port security catches it, and an err-disabled port is what greets you at the cabinet. A patch lead looped between two outlets floods the VLAN: storm control limits the damage. Meraki MS switches offer the same ideas as dashboard settings, such as blocking DHCP servers.

## Self-test

1. After DHCP snooping is enabled for VLAN 10, no client gets an address. What is the most likely cause?
2. Which table does DAI rely on, and what happens to a printer with a static IP on an untrusted port?
3. Name the three port security violation modes. Which one err-disables the port?
4. A port has `switchport port-security maximum 2` and `violation restrict`, yet any number of devices work. What is missing?
5. Which feature stops a PC announcing itself as the IPv6 default gateway, and where is it applied?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The port towards the DHCP server is not trusted, so its OFFER and ACK are dropped.
2. The DHCP snooping binding table. The printer has no binding, so its ARP is dropped.
3. Protect, restrict and shutdown. Only shutdown (the default) err-disables the port.
4. The plain `switchport port-security` command that turns the feature on.
5. RA guard, on host-facing access ports.

</details>

# 5.1 Agentic AI in Network Operations

> **Blueprint 5.1:** Describe the role of agentic AI in network operations

## Summary

Agentic AI works towards a goal over several steps. It plans, calls tools or APIs, checks the results and adapts, with limited human prompting. In network operations it can triage an alert, collect show output, suggest a root cause and draft a fix. Generative AI is a well-read colleague on the phone who can only talk. Agentic AI is a junior engineer with a login: fast, useful and in need of supervision. The exam may ask you to judge an assistant's output against real device output.

## Key facts and defaults

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Predictive AI | Forecasts or classifies from past data |
| Generative AI | Creates content from a prompt. It only returns output |
| Agentic AI | Pursues a goal: plans, calls tools, checks results, adapts |
| Digital network assistant | An AI helper in a management tool that answers questions about your network |
| Human in the loop | A person approves before any change is made |
| Least privilege | Only the access the task needs, read-only where possible |
| Audit logging | Every action the agent takes is recorded |
| Hallucination | Confident but false output, such as a command that does not exist |

## IOS commands

No configuration is in scope. You check an assistant's claims with show commands you already know: `show interfaces`, `show ip interface brief`, `show ip route`, `show logging` and `show running-config`.

## Verification

A user on SW1 port Gi0/1 has no network. The assistant reports:

```
Finding: Gi0/1 on SW1 is shut down.
Recommended change:
  interface GigabitEthernet0/1
   no shutdown
Confidence: high
```

Check it against the device before you approve anything:

```
SW1# show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/1 | include line protocol
GigabitEthernet0/1 is down, line protocol is down (notconnect)

SW1# show running-config interface GigabitEthernet0/1
Building configuration...

Current configuration : 86 bytes
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 switchport access vlan 20
 switchport mode access
end
```

What to look for:

- Does the claim match the output? A shut port reads `administratively down`. This one reads `notconnect`, so the finding is wrong.
- Is there supporting evidence? The config has no `shutdown` line.
- Is the command valid and safe? `no shutdown` is harmless here, but it fixes nothing.
- What is the real next step? `notconnect` means no link signal: check the cable, the patching and the far-end device.

## Exam traps

- Agentic is not generative. A generative tool returns text. An agent takes actions with tools.
- A confident tone is not evidence. Only device output is evidence.
- Human in the loop means approval before the change, not reading the log afterwards.
- Full admin rights for an agent breaks least privilege. Diagnosis needs read-only access.

## On real sites

Cloud dashboards are adding AI assistants and root cause hints. Treat any suggestion like a message from a remote colleague who has not seen the cabinet. Before acting, check the port status and event log in the dashboard (the equivalent of `show interfaces` and `show logging`), or put a tester on the cable.

## Self-test

1. What three things does an agentic AI do that a plain chatbot does not?
2. An assistant says a port is shut down. Which exact words in `show interfaces` would confirm it?
3. Name three guardrails for an AI agent that can change device config.
4. Which type of AI forecasts that a link will fail next week from its error history?
5. An assistant recommends a command that IOS rejects as invalid. What is this called, and what should you have done first?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. It plans several steps, calls tools or APIs, and checks the results and adapts.
2. `administratively down`. Anything else, such as `notconnect`, points to a different fault.
3. Human approval before changes, least privilege access and audit logging.
4. Predictive AI.
5. A hallucination. Verify the recommendation against real device output before acting on it.

</details>

title: 5.2 Selecting a Prompt for Generative AI
md:
# 5.2 Selecting a Prompt for Generative AI

> **Blueprint 5.2:** Select a prompt to send to a generative AI system to support network operations considering prompt components such as data classification, output format, persona, and instructions

## Summary

A prompt is the request you send to a generative AI tool, and the answer is only as good as the prompt. A good prompt gives a role, a clear task, context and the format you want back, and contains nothing too sensitive for that tool. It is like a ticket to a vendor's support desk: a vague ticket gets a vague reply, and you would never paste the customer's passwords into it.

## Key facts and defaults

| Component | What it means |
|---|---|
| Persona | The role the AI takes, such as "senior Cisco network engineer" |
| Instructions | The exact task and its limits |
| Context | Platform, topology, symptoms, what you have tried |
| Output format | Table, numbered steps, IOS commands only, JSON |
| Data classification | How sensitive the data is, and so which tools may see it |

Typical labels: public, internal, confidential, restricted (names vary by employer). Only public data goes into a public AI tool.

Never paste these into a public tool:

- Passwords, enable secrets and password hashes. Type 7 passwords are trivially reversed.
- SNMP community strings, Wi-Fi and VPN pre-shared keys, API keys, private keys.
- Customer names, site addresses, real public IP addresses, full topology.
- Personal data, and any config that has not been sanitised.

## IOS commands

No IOS configuration is in scope. Terms worth recognising: persona, context, sanitise (redact), hallucination. To sanitise, remove secrets and swap real names and addresses for generic ones, such as R1 and 192.0.2.1.

## Verification

A weak prompt:

```
ospf not working pls fix
[entire running-config pasted, with secrets and public IPs]
```

A strong prompt for the same fault:

```
Act as a senior Cisco network engineer.

Context: two IOS XE routers, R1 and R2, share the link
10.0.12.0/30 in OSPF area 0. The neighbour never reaches
FULL. The output below is sanitised: no passwords, and
the names and addresses are generic.

Task: list the three most likely causes, most likely
first. For each one, give a show command that confirms
it. Do not suggest configuration changes yet. Say so if
you are unsure.

Output format: a table with the columns Cause, Check
and Expected result.

Data:
[sanitised output of show ip ospf neighbor and
 show ip ospf interface GigabitEthernet0/0]
```

What to look for:

- The strong prompt has persona, instructions, context and output format, and its data is sanitised.
- The task has limits ("three causes", "no changes yet"), so the answer can be checked.
- The weak prompt fails twice: it is vague, and it leaks confidential data.

## Exam traps

- A prompt containing a password, key or customer data is the wrong choice, however well written.
- The longest option is not always the best. Look for the components, not the word count.
- A persona improves focus, not accuracy. Still verify the answer.
- An approved private AI tool may accept data a public one must not see. Company policy decides.

## On real sites

Dashboard exports and screenshots carry customer and site names, serial numbers, public WAN addresses, Wi-Fi keys and API keys. Strip these before you ask an AI tool about a Meraki or Peplink fault, just as you would sanitise an IOS running-config. Describe the kit generically, such as "a cloud-managed switch uplinked to a dual-WAN router".

## Self-test

1. Name the four prompt components listed in the blueprint.
2. Why is "fix my network" a weak prompt? Give two reasons.
3. You want to paste part of a running-config into a public AI tool. What must you do first?
4. Two prompts are equally clear, but one includes the SNMP community string. Which do you select?
5. Improve this instruction: "tell me about VLANs on my switch".

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Data classification, output format, persona and instructions.
2. It gives no context (platform, symptoms) and no specific task or output format.
3. Sanitise it: remove passwords, hashes, keys and community strings, and replace real names and addresses.
4. The one without it. A community string is a credential.
5. For example: "Act as a Cisco engineer. From the sanitised show vlan brief output below, list the ports in VLAN 20 as a table."

</details>

# 5.3 Network Management Approaches

> **Blueprint 5.3:** Describe network management approaches (device-based, cloud-based, controller-based, automation-based, and infrastructure as code)

## Summary

The five approaches differ in where the configuration lives and who or what applies it: an engineer on each box, a central dashboard or controller, a script, or version-controlled files. Think of a restaurant chain: you can phone each chef (device-based), have head office send the menu to every branch (cloud or controller), or keep one master recipe book that every kitchen is built from (infrastructure as code).

## Key facts and defaults

| Approach | What it means |
|---|---|
| Device-based | CLI or GUI, box by box. Config lives on each device |
| Cloud-based | Vendor-hosted dashboard. Devices call out to it over the internet |
| Controller-based | A central controller holds policy and programs devices through APIs |
| Automation-based | Scripts and tools (Python, Ansible) push changes to many devices |
| Infrastructure as code | Desired state in text files under version control (Git), applied by tools |

- **Planes:** control decides where traffic goes, data forwards it, management is how you configure and monitor.
- **Northbound API:** controller up to applications and scripts, usually REST.
- **Southbound API:** controller down to devices (NETCONF, RESTCONF, SSH, SNMP, OpenFlow).
- **Configuration drift:** devices slowly differ from the standard through one-off manual changes.

## IOS commands

No configuration is in scope. Terms worth recognising: CLI over SSH or console, dashboard, controller, REST API, NETCONF, RESTCONF, playbook, YAML, JSON, Git, source of truth.

## Verification

The same change, add VLAN 30, done two ways. Device-based, repeated on every switch:

```
SW1# configure terminal
SW1(config)# vlan 30
SW1(config-vlan)# name VOICE
SW1(config-vlan)# end
SW1# show vlan id 30
```

Infrastructure as code, one file change that a tool applies to every switch:

```
# vlans.yml, stored in Git
vlans:
  - id: 20
    name: DATA
  - id: 30
    name: VOICE
```

What to look for:

- Typing commands on one device at a time is device-based, even over SSH.
- A file describing the end state, kept in version control, is infrastructure as code.
- A script that logs in and runs a list of commands is automation-based.
- A central system that owns policy and programs devices through APIs is controller-based. If the vendor hosts it on the internet, it is cloud-based.

## Exam traps

- Cloud-based moves the management plane to the cloud. The data plane stays on the device.
- Northbound faces applications. Southbound faces devices.
- Automation alone is not infrastructure as code. IaC needs the desired state in version-controlled files.
- Controller-based means the controller is the intended place to make changes, not that the CLI has gone.

## On real sites

Meraki and Peplink InControl are cloud-based management: devices call out to a vendor-hosted dashboard, and you rarely need a console cable. A Meraki network keeps forwarding traffic if it loses contact with the cloud, but you cannot push changes until it returns. That is the management and data plane split in practice. Plugging a laptop into a console port in the cabinet is pure device-based management.

## Self-test

1. Which approach describes the Meraki dashboard, and where does the configuration live?
2. A controller sends config to switches using NETCONF. Northbound or southbound?
3. What turns "automation" into "infrastructure as code"?
4. A site loses its internet link. Users on a cloud-managed switch can still reach the local server. Which plane still works, and which is lost?
5. What is configuration drift, and which approach suffers from it most?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Cloud-based. The configuration is held in the vendor's cloud and downloaded by the devices.
2. Southbound: from the controller down to the devices.
3. The desired state is written in files kept in version control, so changes are tracked and repeatable.
4. The data plane keeps forwarding. The management plane (contact with the dashboard) is lost.
5. Devices slowly differing from the standard through one-off manual changes. Device-based suffers most.

</details>

# 5.4 SNMP

> **Blueprint 5.4:** Describe the function of SNMP in network operations

## Summary

Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) lets a central monitoring station read values from network devices, such as interface counters, CPU load and uptime, and lets devices raise alerts when something happens. One system can then watch hundreds of devices without anyone logging in to each. It works like a building management panel: the panel polls every sensor on a schedule, and a sensor can also raise an alarm on its own without being asked.

## Key facts and defaults

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Manager (NMS) | The monitoring station. Polls and receives alerts |
| Agent | Software on the device |
| MIB | The database of variables |
| OID | The address of one variable in the MIB |
| UDP 161 | Manager polls the agent (Get and Set) |
| UDP 162 | Agent sends Traps and Informs to the manager |
| Manager to agent | Get, GetNext, GetBulk, Set |
| Agent to manager | Trap (not acknowledged), Inform (acknowledged) |
| v1 and v2c | Community strings, sent in clear text |
| v3 | Users with authentication and encryption |

- **SNMPv3 levels:** noAuthNoPriv (neither), authNoPriv (authentication only), authPriv (both).
- **Community types:** read-only (RO) allows Get. Read-write (RW) also allows Set.

## IOS commands

No configuration is in scope. Commands worth recognising:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `snmp-server community NAME ro` | Sets a read-only community string |
| `snmp-server host 192.0.2.50 version 2c NAME` | Sets where traps are sent |
| `snmp-server enable traps` | Turns on trap sending |
| `show snmp` | Shows SNMP counters and status |

## Verification

```
R1# show snmp
Chassis: FDO2134X0AB
Contact: NOC
Location: Comms room 1
1482 SNMP packets input
    0 Bad SNMP version errors
    3 Unknown community name
    0 Illegal operation for community name supplied
    0 Encoding errors
    2958 Number of requested variables
    0 Number of altered variables
    1100 Get-request PDUs
    379 Get-next PDUs
    0 Set-request PDUs
    0 Input queue packet drops (Maximum queue size 1000)
1491 SNMP packets output
    0 Too big errors (Maximum packet size 1500)
    0 No such name errors
    0 Bad values errors
    0 General errors
    1479 Response PDUs
    12 Trap PDUs
SNMP logging: enabled
    Logging to 192.0.2.50.162, 0/10, 12 sent, 0 dropped.
```

What to look for:

- Rising Get-request and Get-next counters mean a manager is polling this device.
- `Unknown community name` above zero means a poll used the wrong string: an NMS typo, or a probe.
- `Set-request` and `altered variables` at zero mean nothing was changed through SNMP.
- `Trap PDUs` and the `Logging to` line show traps going to the manager on port 162.

## Exam traps

- Port 161 is on the agent (polling). Port 162 is on the manager (traps and informs). Both are UDP.
- A Trap is not acknowledged, so it can be lost. An Inform is acknowledged.
- The "c" in v2c stands for community. It has no encryption.
- authNoPriv authenticates but does not encrypt. Only authPriv does both.
- MIB is the whole database. OID is one entry in it.

## On real sites

The Meraki dashboard and InControl do the job of an SNMP manager for their own kit: usage graphs, uptime history and email alerts are the cloud equivalent of polling and traps. SNMP matters when a customer's own monitoring system must watch mixed-vendor equipment. Meraki and Peplink devices can generally be polled by SNMP too, but check the product documentation for the settings. Treat a community string as a password.

## Self-test

1. Which device listens on UDP 161 and which on UDP 162?
2. What is the difference between a Trap and an Inform?
3. A security audit says SNMPv2c must go. Why, and what replaces it?
4. An NMS can read interface counters but cannot change the device's contact name. What is the likely reason?
5. What are a MIB and an OID?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The agent (the device) listens on 161. The manager listens on 162 for traps and informs.
2. Both are sent by the agent without being asked. Only the Inform is acknowledged by the manager.
3. v2c sends its community string in clear text with no encryption. SNMPv3 with authPriv replaces it.
4. The NMS is using a read-only community, which allows Get but not Set.
5. The MIB is the database of variables an agent can report. An OID is the address of one variable in it.

</details>

# 5.5 Ansible

> **Blueprint 5.5:** Use configuration management mechanisms such as Ansible to execute commands

## Summary

Ansible is a configuration management tool that runs commands on many devices from one machine. It is agentless: nothing is installed on the routers and switches, and Ansible connects to them over SSH. You list your devices in an inventory, write what you want done in a YAML playbook, and Ansible does it on every device and reports back. It is like handing the same job sheet to a team of engineers who visit every site at once and return a signed report.

## Key facts and defaults

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Model | Agentless, push model over SSH |
| Control node | The machine that runs Ansible |
| Managed nodes | The devices it connects to |
| Inventory | The list of hosts and groups |
| Playbook | YAML file of plays. Each play has tasks |
| Module | The code a task runs to do the work |
| `cisco.ios.ios_command` | Runs exec commands, mainly show commands |
| `cisco.ios.ios_config` | Applies configuration lines |
| Ad-hoc command | One module run from the shell, no playbook |
| Idempotent | Running again makes no further change |

YAML rules: indent with spaces, never tabs. `key: value` needs a space after the colon. A list item starts with a dash and a space.

## IOS commands

The devices only need SSH and a login. Everything else is typed on the control node. A small inventory, `inventory.ini`:

```
[routers]
R1 ansible_host=192.168.10.1
R2 ansible_host=192.168.10.2

[routers:vars]
ansible_connection=ansible.netcommon.network_cli
ansible_network_os=cisco.ios.ios
ansible_user=admin
```

A playbook, `uptime.yml`:

```
---
- name: Check router uptime
  hosts: routers
  gather_facts: false

  tasks:
    - name: Run a show command
      cisco.ios.ios_command:
        commands:
          - show version | include uptime
      register: result

    - name: Print the output
      ansible.builtin.debug:
        var: result.stdout_lines
```

Run the playbook, then a single ad-hoc command:

```
ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini uptime.yml -k

ansible routers -i inventory.ini -k \
  -m cisco.ios.ios_command -a "commands='show clock'"
```

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `-i` | Names the inventory file |
| `-k` | Prompts for the SSH password |
| `-m` and `-a` | Module and its arguments (ad-hoc) |
| `--syntax-check` | Checks the playbook without running it |

## Verification

```
$ ansible-playbook -i inventory.ini uptime.yml -k
SSH password:

PLAY [Check router uptime] *********************************

TASK [Run a show command] **********************************
ok: [R1]
ok: [R2]

TASK [Print the output] ************************************
ok: [R1] => {
    "result.stdout_lines": [
        [
            "R1 uptime is 3 weeks, 2 days, 4 hours, 17 minutes"
        ]
    ]
}
ok: [R2] => {
    "result.stdout_lines": [
        [
            "R2 uptime is 1 day, 6 hours, 52 minutes"
        ]
    ]
}

PLAY RECAP *************************************************
R1  : ok=2  changed=0  unreachable=0  failed=0
R2  : ok=2  changed=0  unreachable=0  failed=0
```

The recap is trimmed to fit a phone screen. Real output is wider.

What to look for:

- `ok` means the task ran and changed nothing. Show commands should give `changed=0`.
- `changed` means the device was altered. Expect it from `ios_config`, not `ios_command`.
- `unreachable` means Ansible could not connect. `failed` means the task hit an error.

## Exam traps

- Ansible is agentless and pushes over SSH. Reject any answer that installs an agent on the device.
- `ios_command` is for exec commands. Configuration lines belong in `ios_config`.
- `hosts:` in the play must match a host or group name in the inventory.
- YAML is indentation-sensitive. A tab or a badly indented task breaks the playbook.
- `ansible` runs ad-hoc commands. `ansible-playbook` runs playbooks.

## On real sites

Applying one Meraki configuration template or one InControl group setting to many sites is the same idea as a playbook: define it once, apply it everywhere. The dashboard does the pushing for cloud-managed kit. Ansible does it over SSH for the IOS switches and routers you cannot manage from a dashboard. Running one show command across every device is a quick way to audit uptime or software versions before a site visit.

## Self-test

1. What does agentless mean, and which protocol does Ansible use to reach an IOS device?
2. Which file lists the devices, and which lists the tasks?
3. Which module runs `show ip route`, and which adds a VLAN?
4. A play recap shows `ok=2 changed=0`. What does that tell you?
5. Write the ad-hoc command that runs `show clock` on the group `routers` using `inventory.ini`.

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. No software is installed on the managed device. Ansible connects from the control node over SSH.
2. The inventory lists devices and groups. The playbook lists plays and tasks.
3. `cisco.ios.ios_command` runs the show command. `cisco.ios.ios_config` applies configuration such as a VLAN.
4. Two tasks ran successfully and nothing on the device was changed.
5. `ansible routers -i inventory.ini -k -m cisco.ios.ios_command -a "commands='show clock'"`

</details>

# 5.6 Syslog

> **Blueprint 5.6:** Interpret syslog message content, severity levels, and facilities

## Summary

Syslog is how a network device reports events: an interface going down, a config change, a failed login. Each message says when it happened, which part of the system raised it, how serious it is and what occurred. Messages can go to the console, a memory buffer or a syslog server on UDP 514. It is the device's logbook, like the event log on an alarm panel.

## Key facts and defaults

One message (a single line on the device, wrapped here to fit):

```
*Mar  1 00:14:06.118: %LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN: Line protocol on
  Interface GigabitEthernet0/1, changed state to up
```

| Field | In the example |
|---|---|
| Timestamp | `*Mar  1 00:14:06.118` |
| Facility | `LINEPROTO`, the IOS component that raised it |
| Severity | `5`, notifications |
| Mnemonic | `UPDOWN`, a short code for the event |
| Description | The text after the last colon |

| Level | Keyword | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | emergencies | System unusable |
| 1 | alerts | Act immediately |
| 2 | critical | Critical |
| 3 | errors | Error |
| 4 | warnings | Warning |
| 5 | notifications | Normal but significant |
| 6 | informational | Information only |
| 7 | debugging | Debug output |

- **Destinations:** console (on by default), terminal lines (`terminal monitor`), the internal buffer (`logging buffered`), a syslog server (`logging host`).
- **Facility, two meanings:** in the message it is the IOS component (LINK, LINEPROTO, SYS, OSPF). On a syslog server it is the category messages are filed under, `local7` by default.
- **Default trap level:** informational (6).

## IOS commands

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `logging host 192.0.2.50` | Sends messages to a syslog server |
| `logging trap warnings` | Sends levels 0 to 4 to the server |
| `logging buffered` | Keeps messages in memory |
| `terminal monitor` | Shows messages on your SSH session |
| `show logging` | Shows the settings and the buffer |

`logging trap` with a level sends that level and every more severe one (lower numbers). `logging trap 4` equals `logging trap warnings`.

## Verification

```
R1# show logging | include level|Logging to
    Console logging: level debugging, 45 messages logged, xml disabled,
    Monitor logging: level debugging, 0 messages logged, xml disabled,
    Buffer logging:  level debugging, 45 messages logged, xml disabled,
    Trap logging: level warnings, 12 message lines logged
        Logging to 192.0.2.50  (udp port 514, audit disabled,
```

Plain `show logging` ends with the buffer (long lines wrapped here):

```
*Mar  1 00:14:05.118: %LINK-3-UPDOWN: Interface
  GigabitEthernet0/1, changed state to up
*Mar  1 00:14:06.118: %LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN: Line protocol on
  Interface GigabitEthernet0/1, changed state to up
```

What to look for:

- `Trap logging: level warnings` means only levels 0 to 4 reach the server. So 12 lines were sent, but 45 were logged locally.
- Of the two buffer messages, the server receives LINK-3 but not LINEPROTO-5.
- A `*` before the timestamp means the clock is not synchronised. Fix NTP before comparing logs between devices.

## Exam traps

- Lower number means more severe.
- `logging trap 4` sends 0 to 4, not 4 to 7.
- "Trap" here is a syslog setting. It is not an SNMP trap.
- An SSH session shows no log messages until you type `terminal monitor`.
- `%LINK-3-UPDOWN` is the physical link. `%LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN` is the line protocol. Their severities differ.

## On real sites

The event logs in the Meraki dashboard and on a Peplink router are the same idea as `show logging`: time-stamped entries for ports going up and down and WAN failover. Both can generally forward events to a syslog server too (check the product documentation). When a customer says "it dropped at about ten past nine", the log is your proof.

## Self-test

1. Break down `%SYS-5-CONFIG_I` into its three parts.
2. Which levels does `logging trap errors` send to the server?
3. You are on SSH and see no log messages, but a colleague on the console does. What do you type?
4. A message starts `*Mar  1 00:02:11.004`. What does the `*` tell you, and what should you fix?
5. Which is more severe, level 2 or level 6, and what are their keywords?

<details>
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. Facility SYS, severity 5 (notifications), mnemonic CONFIG_I (the device was configured).
2. Levels 0 to 3: emergencies, alerts, critical and errors.
3. `terminal monitor`, in privileged exec mode.
4. The clock is not synchronised. Configure NTP.
5. Level 2 (critical). Level 6 is informational. Lower numbers are more severe.

</details>

# Lab 01 - Basic Switch and Router Setup, and SSH

**Blueprint:** 4.1 (local usernames for management), 2.4 (show commands and ping)
**Time:** 30-40 minutes
**Tool:** Cisco Packet Tracer

## Objective

Take a router and a switch from factory default to a state where you would be happy to leave them on a
customer site: named, password protected, reachable over SSH only, and saved. This is the IOS equivalent
of claiming a device into a Meraki dashboard and setting the admin accounts, except you do every step
by hand.

## Topology

```
 PC1 ---------------- SW1 ---------------- R1
 (FastEthernet0)   Fa0/1   Gi0/1        Gi0/0
```

| Device | Model in Packet Tracer | Link |
|---|---|---|
| R1 | 2911 router | Gi0/0 to SW1 Gi0/1 |
| SW1 | 2960 switch | Fa0/1 to PC1 |
| PC1 | PC | FastEthernet0 to SW1 Fa0/1 |

Use copper straight-through cables. Connect a console (rollover) cable from PC1's RS-232 port to each
device in turn when you configure it, and use the PC's **Terminal** app. That is how you would do it on
site.

## Addressing table

| Device | Interface | IP address | Mask | Default gateway |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | Gi0/0 | 192.168.10.1 | 255.255.255.0 | - |
| SW1 | VLAN 1 (SVI) | 192.168.10.2 | 255.255.255.0 | 192.168.10.1 |
| PC1 | NIC | 192.168.10.10 | 255.255.255.0 | 192.168.10.1 |

## Tasks

Do these on **R1 first**, then repeat on **SW1**. Try each one from memory. Use `?` freely: learning to
find a command with `?` is part of the skill.

1. Enter privileged EXEC mode, then global configuration mode.
2. Set the hostname (R1 / SW1).
3. Stop the device trying to resolve mistyped commands as hostnames.
4. Set an encrypted privileged-mode password of `Class123!`.
5. Create a local user `admin` with privilege level 15 and the hashed password `Cisco123!`.
6. Set the domain name to `lab.local`.
7. Generate an RSA key pair with a 2048-bit modulus.
8. Force SSH version 2.
9. On the console line: require a local username login, and stop log messages interrupting your typing.
10. On vty lines 0 to 4: require a local username login, allow SSH only, and time out idle sessions
    after 5 minutes.
11. Set a message-of-the-day banner that warns against unauthorised access.
12. Configure the IP address:
    - R1: on Gi0/0, and bring the interface up.
    - SW1: on the VLAN 1 interface, bring it up, and set the default gateway.
13. Encrypt any clear-text passwords in the configuration.
14. Save the configuration.
15. Configure PC1 with its address, mask and gateway.

## Verification

Run each command and compare with the expected result. If yours differs, work out why before moving on.

| # | Where | Command | Expected result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | R1 | `show ip interface brief` | Gi0/0 has 192.168.10.1, Status `up`, Protocol `up` |
| 2 | SW1 | `show ip interface brief` | Vlan1 has 192.168.10.2, Status `up`, Protocol `up` |
| 3 | PC1 | `ping 192.168.10.1` and `ping 192.168.10.2` | Replies from both (the first ping may time out while ARP completes) |
| 4 | R1 | `show ip ssh` | `SSH Enabled - version 2.0` |
| 5 | PC1 | `ssh -l admin 192.168.10.1` | Password prompt, then the `R1#` prompt (privilege 15 lands you in enable mode) |
| 6 | PC1 | `telnet 192.168.10.1` | Connection refused or closed. Telnet must NOT work |
| 7 | R1 | `show running-config` | No password is readable in clear text. `enable secret` and the username show hashes |
| 8 | R1 | `show startup-config` | Matches the running configuration (proves you saved) |
| 9 | R1 | `show users` (while the SSH session is open) | A `vty` line in use by `admin` from 192.168.10.10 |

**Questions to answer in your own words** (tell Claude your answers):

- Why did you need a hostname and a domain name before generating the keys?
- What is the difference between `enable secret` and `enable password`? Which wins if both exist?
- The switch is a Layer 2 device. Why does it need an IP address and a default gateway at all?
- What does `login local` do that plain `login` does not?

## Break it

Do these one at a time. After each one, try to SSH from PC1, observe the symptom, find the cause using
only `show` commands, and fix it.

1. On R1: `line vty 0 4`, then `transport input telnet`.
2. On R1: `interface gi0/0`, then `shutdown`.
3. On SW1: `no ip default-gateway`. (PC1 can still reach SW1. Why? When would this fault actually
   matter? Hint: think about where the management PC would have to be.)
4. On R1: `no username admin`. What happens to a session that is already open? What about a new one?

For each fault, write down: the symptom, the show command that revealed it, and the fix.

---
---

## SOLUTION

**Stop. Only read below this line after you have attempted every task and every break-it fault.**

---
---

### R1

```
enable
configure terminal
hostname R1
no ip domain-lookup
enable secret Class123!
username admin privilege 15 secret Cisco123!
ip domain-name lab.local
crypto key generate rsa
 (answer 2048 when asked for the modulus; on newer IOS: crypto key generate rsa modulus 2048)
ip ssh version 2
line console 0
 login local
 logging synchronous
 exit
line vty 0 4
 login local
 transport input ssh
 exec-timeout 5 0
 exit
banner motd #Authorised access only. Activity is logged.#
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
 exit
service password-encryption
end
copy running-config startup-config
```

### SW1

Identical to R1 for steps 1 to 11 (use `hostname SW1`), then:

```
interface vlan 1
 ip address 192.168.10.2 255.255.255.0
 no shutdown
 exit
ip default-gateway 192.168.10.1
service password-encryption
end
copy running-config startup-config
```

### Notes on the commands

- `no ip domain-lookup` and `ip domain-name` are the spellings Packet Tracer accepts. Current IOS XE
  also accepts (and displays) `no ip domain lookup` and `ip domain name`. Know both.
- A router interface is shut down by default. A switch port is not, but the VLAN 1 SVI is.
- `ip default-gateway` is for a Layer 2 switch. A router, or a switch with `ip routing` enabled, uses a
  default route instead.

### Answers to the questions

- The RSA key pair is named `hostname.domain-name`, so IOS needs both before it can create the keys.
- `enable secret` is stored as a hash; `enable password` is clear text (or weak type 7 with
  `service password-encryption`). If both exist, the secret is the one that works.
- The address is for managing the switch itself (SSH, SNMP, syslog). The gateway lets it reply to
  management stations on other subnets.
- `login local` checks the local username database. Plain `login` asks only for the line password.

### Break-it answers

| # | Symptom | Revealed by | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | SSH connection closed immediately; Telnet now works | `show running-config \| begin line vty` shows `transport input telnet` | `line vty 0 4`, `transport input ssh` |
| 2 | Ping and SSH to R1 time out | `show ip interface brief`: Gi0/0 `administratively down / down` | `interface gi0/0`, `no shutdown` |
| 3 | Nothing visible from PC1, because PC1 is in the same subnet. From any other subnet the switch could not reply | `show running-config \| include default-gateway` returns nothing | `ip default-gateway 192.168.10.1` |
| 4 | The open session carries on. New logins fail: no such user | `show running-config \| include username` | Re-create the user. On a real site, never remove the last admin account while you are remote |

## 2. Domains and weightings

## 3. Objectives and status

### 1.0 Network Infrastructure and Connectivity (25%)

| 1.1 | Diagnose interface and cable (copper and fiber) issues such as collisions, errors, mismatched duplex, speed, distance, interface, signal levels, pin out, and cable types |

### 2.0 Switching and Network Access (25%)

| ID | Official objective |
|---|---|
| 2.1 | Configure network infrastructure connectivity (switch-to-switch and switch-to-router) |
| 2.1.a | Layer 2/Layer 3 physical interfaces |

| 2.1.c | Layer 2/Layer 3 LACP port-channel/EtherChannel |
| 2.1.d | Switch virtual interface (SVI) |

| ID | Official objective |
|---|---|
| 3.1 | Interpret a routing table to identify the next hop for a packet (routing protocol, prefix/mask, administrative distance, metric, and default route) |

| 5.3 | Describe network management approaches (device-based, cloud-based, controller-based, automation-based, and infrastructure as code) |
| 5.4 | Describe the function of SNMP in network operations |
| 5.5 | Use configuration management mechanisms such as Ansible to execute commands |
| 5.6 | Interpret syslog message content, severity levels, and facilities |

---

## 4. What the verbs tell us

Cisco chooses its verbs carefully. They tell you how deep each topic goes.

| Verb | What the exam expects | Where it appears |
|---|---|---|
| Describe | Know what it is and why it exists. No configuration. | 1.2, 1.5, 4.5, 5.1, 5.3, 5.4 |
| Interpret | Read real output and draw the right conclusion. | 3.1, 3.4, 5.6 |
| Validate / Select / Use | Apply a tool or make a judgement call. | 2.3, 5.2, 5.5 |
| Configure | Type the commands from memory and verify them. | 2.1, 2.2, 2.5, 3.3, 4.1, 4.3, 4.6, 4.7 |
| Manage | Carry out an operational task (file transfer). | 4.2 |
| Diagnose / Troubleshoot | Find and fix a fault from symptoms and show output. Hardest level. | 1.1, 1.3, 1.4, 1.6, 1.7, 2.4, 3.2, 4.4 |

**Count:** 8 of the 29 objectives are Diagnose/Troubleshoot and 8 are Configure. v2.0 is a hands-on,
fault-finding exam. That suits your site experience, but it means the IOS CLI must become second nature.

---

## 5. How v2.0 differs from v1.1

Compared directly against Cisco's official v1.1 exam topics PDF (read 24 November 2026).

| | v1.1 | v2.0 |
|---|---|---|
| Domains | 6 | 5 |
| Top-level objectives | 53 | 29 |
| Describe / explain / compare objectives | 32 | 6 |
| Troubleshoot / diagnose objectives | 0 | 8 |

**New in v2.0 (not in v1.1):**

- OSPFv3 for IPv6 (3.3) and VRRP named alongside HSRP (3.4)
- Storm control and RA guard (4.7)
- Diagnosing DNS records: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, NS, PTR (4.4)
- SFTP/SCP file management (4.2), replacing "describe TFTP/FTP"
- Configuring a device as an AAA client for TACACS+ and RADIUS (4.1)
- Packet capture output and extended ping (2.4)
- Switch ports for APs, phones, virtualised hosts and appliances, including PoE (2.2)
- Troubleshooting a DHCPv4 server on IOS (1.7)
- Agentic AI (5.1), choosing an AI prompt (5.2), infrastructure as code (5.3), using Ansible to run commands (5.5)

**Already in v1.1, but raised a level in v2.0:**

| Topic | v1.1 verb | v2.0 verb |
|---|---|---|
| Rapid PVST+ | Interpret | Configure |
| Interface and cable issues | Identify | Diagnose |
| IPv4 and IPv6 addressing | Configure and verify | Troubleshoot |
| Static routing | Configure and verify | Troubleshoot |
| First hop redundancy | Describe | Interpret the operational status |
| Client IP settings (Windows, macOS, Linux) | Verify | Troubleshoot |

**In v1.1 but NOT listed in v2.0:**

| Topic | Approach in this course |
|---|---|
| NTP | Short lab only. A related topic (syslog timestamps depend on it). |
| Wireless LAN controller GUI setup, wireless architectures and AP modes | One light lab for context. Low priority. |
| Network components, topology architectures, TCP vs UDP, switching concepts as theory | Not objectives any more, but assumed knowledge. Covered in Phase 2 as foundations. |
| QoS, REST APIs, JSON, Terraform, overlay/underlay/fabric | Skip unless time allows. |
| Security programme concepts, password policy | Skip. |
| TFTP/FTP | Known as the insecure contrast to SCP/SFTP only. |


Remember Cisco's own warning: "additional related topics may be included in any given exam version".
We treat the listed objectives as the priority and the related topics as cheap insurance.

## Checkpoints

- End of week 6: subnetting under 30 seconds at 90%+, and comfortable in the command line.
- End of week 10: half mock at 65%+.
- End of week 14: half mock at 75%+. Book the exam after this one.
- End of week 17: full mock 1 at 80%+.

Miss a checkpoint and the exam date moves. That is the plan working, not failing.

## Ready means all five

- Three full mock exams in a row at 90% or above
- Every blueprint objective marked Exam-ready
- Subnetting under 20 seconds average with 95%+ accuracy
- Every capstone lab completed without the solution
- 9 out of 10 troubleshooting scenarios solved
